Haughton Crater.why: About 20 km impact crater in a cold polar desert; long-running NASA analog site.
Haughton Crater.breaks: 24-hour sun during the summer field season, so no lasting shadow while crews are there.
Haughton Crater.helps: Haughton-Mars Project (since 1997, NASA-supported, run by the Mars Institute): field tests of rovers, including a pressurized rover with suit ports, robotic drills, cameras and spectrometers, spacesuit gear such as a smart glove, and long traverses planned like Moon and Mars expeditions.

sources.label: Aerospace Testing International: Testing for Mars in the High Arctic

Atacama (Yungay area).why: One of the driest places on Earth, with very high UV.
Atacama (Yungay area).breaks: Warm and near the tropics: no polar lighting and no long shadows.
Atacama (Yungay area).helps: NASA's ARADS project (from 2016) drove the KREX-2 prototype rover near Yungay, drilled up to 2 m and tested life-detection instruments (SOLID, Wet Chemistry Lab) to rehearse a search for life on Mars.

sources.label: NASA Astrobiology: life detection drill in the Atacama (2017)
Space.com: NASA tests life-detecting rover tech in Chile

Meteor Crater.why: About 1.2 km wide impact crater; Apollo astronauts trained in geology here.
Meteor Crater.breaks: Hot desert at mid-latitude: no polar light, far smaller than Shackleton.
Meteor Crater.helps: Apollo astronauts did geology field training here from 1963, taught by USGS scientists such as Gene Shoemaker. The crater is still used to train astronauts for missions to the lunar south pole.

sources.label: USGS: In the footsteps of the Apollo astronauts (field guide)
Phys.org: Training future explorers of the Moon (2018)

Craters of the Moon.why: Young basalt lava field with lava tubes; Apollo astronauts trained here in 1969.
Craters of the Moon.breaks: Young, fresh lava with plants, air and weather. Lunar basalt is buried under fine dust (regolith) built up over billions of years of impacts.
Craters of the Moon.helps: On 22 August 1969, Apollo 14 crew Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell, with Joe Engle and Eugene Cernan, learned volcanic geology here to pick the most valuable rock samples on the Moon. NASA scientists still do research here.

sources.label: National Park Service: Space exploration research and astronaut training

Lava Beds.place: Lava Beds National Monument, California, USA
Lava Beds.why: Hundreds of lava-tube caves in basalt.
Lava Beds.breaks: Earth caves have air, moisture, ice and microbes, and they are much smaller than the lava tubes thought to exist on the Moon.
Lava Beds.helps: NASA Ames's BRAILLE project (2019) drove the CaveR rover in Valentine Cave to map the cave with a laser scanner and look for signs of microbial life on the walls, showing that a remotely operated rover can explore a lava tube.

sources.label: NASA Astrobiology: Using a cave rover, NASA learns to search for life underground (2019)

Lanzarote lava tubes.why: Lava tubes and volcanic plains; ESA trains astronauts in planetary geology on the island.
Lanzarote lava tubes.breaks: Mild ocean climate with air and weather, and a tourist island with roads and towns, so it is far easier to reach than a lunar cave.
Lanzarote lava tubes.helps: ESA's PANGAEA course trains astronauts from ESA, NASA and JAXA in planetary geology here, including work inside the Corona lava tube, one of the largest volcanic caves on Earth.

sources.label: ESA: Turning astronauts into planetary explorers (2023)
Phys.org: 'Like the Moon': astronauts flock to Spanish isle to train (2022)

Rjukan valley.why: Deep east-west valley; the town gets no direct sun for about six months a year.
Rjukan valley.breaks: Green, wet and inhabited: nothing like bare lunar ground.

pinacate r001c002.name: El Elegante crater
pinacate r001c002.place: El Pinacate y Gran Desierto de Altar, Sonora, Mexico
pinacate r001c002.why: A near-circular volcanic crater (maar) about 1.6 km wide and 244 m deep, with steep inner walls and a flat floor: our pipeline's closest bowl after Meteor Crater.
pinacate r001c002.breaks: It is a volcanic maar, made by steam explosions, not an impact crater. Hot, low-latitude desert: no polar light or permanent shadow, and far smaller than Shackleton (about 21 km).
